author: Augustine
text: You made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
original: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
work: Confessions, Book 1 (Pusey translation, modernized)
significance: We were made for God, so no job, success or relationship can satisfy us until we find our rest in him.

author: Augustine
text: Too late I loved You, O Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new!
original: Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new!
work: Confessions, Book 10 (Pusey translation, modernized)
significance: God's beauty is ancient yet always fresh; it is never too late to turn to him, and regret over lost years can fuel love.

author: Augustine
text: Give what You command, and command what You will.
original: Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.
work: Confessions, Book 10 (Pusey translation, modernized)
significance: God never asks us to obey in our own strength; we can pray for the very grace to do what he commands.

author: Augustine
text: Blessed is the one who loves You, and his friend in You, and his enemy for Your sake.
original: Blessed whoso loveth Thee, and his friend in Thee, and his enemy for Thee.
work: Confessions, Book 4 (Pusey translation, modernized)
significance: Loving God reorders every relationship, so we love friends in him and even enemies for his sake.

author: Augustine
text: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
work: The City of God, Book 14, Chapter 28 (Dods translation)
significance: Every life, home and institution is shaped by its deepest love: love of self pushes God out, love of God puts self in its place.

author: John Calvin
text: Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid Wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.
work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 1, Section 1 (Beveridge translation)
significance: True wisdom starts with knowing God and knowing ourselves honestly; each sharpens the other and keeps us humble.

author: John Calvin
text: We are not our own; therefore, as far as possible, let us forget ourselves and the things that are ours. On the other hand, we are God's; let us, therefore, live and die to him.
work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, Chapter 7, Section 1 (Beveridge translation)
significance: Belonging to God frees us from living for ourselves; our time, gifts and plans are his to direct, in life and death.

author: John Calvin
text: Hence we may infer, that the human mind is, so to speak, a perpetual forge of idols.
work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 11, Section 8 (Beveridge translation)
significance: Our hearts constantly manufacture substitutes for God, so we must keep watching what we really trust and love most.

author: John Calvin
text: There is no work so mean and so sordid that does not look truly respectable and highly important in the sight of God.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 94
significance: Ordinary, unseen work done in God's calling has real dignity before him, from the classroom to the kitchen.

author: John Calvin
text: Being humbled, we learn to call upon his strength which alone makes us stand up under such a load of afflictions.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 50
significance: Hardship strips away self-reliance and teaches us to lean on God's strength, which alone can carry us through.

author: Martin Luther
text: Faith is a living, daring confidence in God's grace, so sure and certain that a man would stake his life on it a thousand times.
work: Preface to the Epistle to the Romans (1522; Luther's Works vol. 35)
significance: Faith is not a vague feeling but bold trust in God's grace, strong enough to stake everything on it.

author: Martin Luther
text: That now, I say, upon which you set your heart and put your trust is properly your god.
work: Large Catechism, The First Commandment
significance: Whatever we most rely on for security and meaning functions as our god, so our trust reveals our true worship.

author: Martin Luther
text: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and the grace of God.
work: Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Thesis 62 (Works of Martin Luther, 1915)
significance: The church's greatest wealth is the gospel of God's grace, not its buildings, programs or reputation.

author: Martin Luther
text: Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, when He said Poenitentiam agite, willed that the whole life of believers should be repentance.
work: Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Thesis 1 (Works of Martin Luther, 1915)
significance: Repentance is not a one-time event but the daily pattern of the Christian life, turning again and again to Christ.

author: Martin Luther
text: There is no more lovely, friendly and charming relationship, communion or company than a good marriage.
work: Table Talk, no. 292
significance: A good marriage is one of God's richest gifts, a friendship and companionship worth cherishing and protecting.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, to live with all my might, while I do live.
work: Resolutions, No. 6
significance: Life is short and given by God, so we should give ourselves wholeheartedly to every day and every task.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, never to lose one moment of time, but to improve it in the most profitable way I possibly can.
work: Resolutions, No. 5
significance: Time is a trust from God; using it well, rather than drifting, is part of faithful stewardship.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, never to do any thing, which I should be afraid to do if it were the last hour of my life.
work: Resolutions, No. 7
significance: Living as if this were our last hour keeps us from actions we would be ashamed to bring before God.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, never to give over, nor in the least to slacken, my fight with my corruptions, however unsuccessful I may be.
work: Resolutions, No. 56
significance: Faithfulness means refusing to quit the fight against sin, even when progress seems slow or invisible.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections.
work: Religious Affections, Part 1
significance: Real faith engages the heart, not just the head; love, joy and hope toward God lie at the core of true religion.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: Care more for a grain of faith than a ton of excitement.
work: Lectures to My Students, First Series, Lecture 11
significance: Quiet, genuine trust in God matters far more than emotional highs or outward enthusiasm in ministry and life.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: My trust is not that I am holy, but that, being unholy, Christ died for me.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 592
significance: Our confidence before God rests on Christ's death for sinners, not on our own performance or goodness.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: I would rather go to Heaven doubting all the way than be lost through self-confidence.
work: Sermon 2490, "The Danger of Carnal Security"
significance: Humble, wrestling faith is safer than proud self-assurance; complacency is a greater danger than honest doubt.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: Losses and crosses are heavy to bear; but when our hearts are right with God, it is wonderful how easy the yoke becomes.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 169
significance: Suffering is real and heavy, but a heart at peace with God finds Christ's yoke surprisingly light.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: Jesus was a great worker, and His disciples must not be afraid of hard work.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 128
significance: Christ worked tirelessly for others, so his followers should embrace hard work as part of serving him.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried.
work: What's Wrong with the World, Part 1, Chapter 5, "The Unfinished Temple"
significance: Christianity's failures usually come from not attempting its hard demands, not from the faith itself falling short.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: Joy, which was the small publicity of the pagan, is the gigantic secret of the Christian.
work: Orthodoxy, Chapter 9, "Authority and the Adventurer"
significance: Christian joy runs deeper than worldly cheer; beneath real sorrows lies a settled gladness rooted in God.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.
work: Orthodoxy, Chapter 7, "The Eternal Revolution"
significance: Humility and not taking ourselves too seriously bring freedom and lightness; pride weighs the soul down.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: I would maintain that thanks are the highest form of thought; and that gratitude is happiness doubled by wonder.
work: A Short History of England (1917), p. 59
significance: Gratitude joined with wonder multiplies joy; giving thanks is the fitting response to every gift from God.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: The world will never starve for want of wonders; but only for want of wonder.
work: Tremendous Trifles (1909), Chapter 1
significance: The world is full of God's wonders; what we lack is the attentive, grateful eyes to notice them.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Aim at Heaven and you will get earth 'thrown in': aim at earth and you will get neither.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 3, Chapter 10, "Hope"
significance: When we seek God first, earthly goods fall into their proper place; chasing earthly things alone loses both.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world.
work: The Problem of Pain, Chapter 6, "Human Pain"
significance: God can use pain to wake us from complacency and draw us to himself when gentler means go unheard.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal.
work: "The Weight of Glory" (1941 sermon), in The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses
significance: Every person we meet is an eternal being, which should shape how we teach, lead and treat others.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: To love at all is to be vulnerable. Love anything, and your heart will certainly be wrung and possibly be broken.
work: The Four Loves, Chapter 6, "Charity"
significance: Real love always risks hurt; refusing to love in order to stay safe slowly hardens the heart.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Every Christian is to become a little Christ.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 4, Chapter 4, "Good Infection"
significance: The goal of the Christian life is to be shaped into Christ's likeness, sharing his life with the world.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Gratitude looks to the past and love to the present; fear, avarice, lust, and ambition look ahead.
work: The Screwtape Letters (Screwtape speaking)
significance: Gratitude and love keep us grounded in what God has done and is doing, while anxious ambition lives in the future.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of our Church. We are fighting to-day for costly grace.
work: The Cost of Discipleship (1937; English tr. 1959), p. 43
significance: Grace is free but never cheap; it calls us to follow Christ wholeheartedly rather than excuse ongoing sin.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: Suffering willingly endured is stronger than evil, it spells death to evil.
work: The Cost of Discipleship, p. 142
significance: Patiently bearing wrong, as Christ did, overcomes evil instead of feeding it with retaliation.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: Time is the most precious gift in our possession, for it is the most irrevocable.
work: Letters and Papers from Prison, p. 47
significance: Time cannot be recovered once spent, so every hour deserves careful stewardship before God.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: We are to find God in what we know, not in what we don't know.
work: Letters and Papers from Prison, letter to Eberhard Bethge, 25 May 1944
significance: God is not just a filler for gaps in our knowledge; he is Lord over all of life, including what we understand.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Prayer will consume sin, or sin will choke prayer.
work: A Call to Prayer (1867), p. 16
significance: Prayer and willful sin cannot coexist for long; one will drive out the other, so guard your prayer life.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Knowledge of the Bible never comes by intuition. It can only be got by hard, regular, daily, attentive, wakeful reading.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Matthew, on Matthew 4:1-11
significance: Biblical understanding grows through steady, disciplined daily reading, not shortcuts or sudden insight.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Ignorance of Scripture is the root of every error in religion, and the source of every heresy.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. John, Vol. 1, Preface
significance: Most spiritual error grows from not knowing the Bible well, which is why teaching Scripture matters so much.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: The heart is the part of man which God chiefly notices in religion.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Mark, on Mark 7:1-13
significance: God looks past outward religion to the heart, so our inner motives matter more than appearances.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: The parent who tries to train without setting a good example is building with one hand and pulling down with the other.
work: The Upper Room, Chapter 16, "The Duties of Parents"
significance: Children learn more from what parents do than what they say; a godly example must match godly instruction.

author: John Owen
text: Put sin to death; make it your daily work; keep at it as long as you live; do not stop for a single day; be killing sin or it will be killing you.
original: Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin or it will be killing you.
work: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2 (modernized)
significance: Fighting sin is a daily, lifelong task; if we stop resisting it, sin will quietly destroy our spiritual life.

author: John Owen
text: Let no one think he is making any progress in holiness if he does not walk over the bellies of his lusts.
original: Let not that man think he makes any progress in holiness who walks not over the bellies of his lusts.
work: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2 (modernized)
significance: Real growth in holiness requires actively defeating sinful desires, not merely admiring good ideals.

author: Richard Baxter
text: Watch yourselves, in case your example contradicts your teaching ... in case you undo with your lives what you say with your tongues.
original: Take heed to yourselves, lest your example contradict your doctrine ... lest you unsay with your lives, what you say with your tongues.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1 (modernized)
significance: Leaders must make sure their lives back up their words, or their example will undo their teaching.

author: Richard Baxter
text: Whoever means what he says will surely do what he says.
original: He that means as he speaks, will surely do as he speaks.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1 (modernized)
significance: Sincerity shows itself in action; if we truly mean what we say, our deeds will follow our words.

author: Herman Bavinck
text: The essence of the Christian religion consists in the reality that the creation of the Father, ruined by sin, is restored in the death of the Son of God and re-created by the grace of the Holy Spirit into a kingdom of God.
work: Reformed Dogmatics, Vol. 1: Prolegomena, p. 112
significance: The gospel is God's plan to restore his whole creation through Christ and the Spirit, giving all of life purpose.

author: Augustine
text: Your best servant is the one who is not so eager to hear from You what he himself wants, as to want what he hears from You.
original: He is Thy best servant who looks not so much to hear that from Thee which himself willeth, as rather to will that, which from Thee he heareth.
work: Confessions, Book 10 (Pusey translation, modernized)
significance: Mature prayer seeks to want what God wills rather than to get God to approve what we already want.

author: Augustine
text: Bad times, hard times, this is what people keep saying; but let us live well, and times shall be good. We are the times: Such as we are, such are the times.
work: Sermon 80, section 8
significance: Instead of blaming the age, Christians shape their times by how faithfully they live in their homes, schools and work.

author: Augustine
text: Since you cannot do good to all, you are to pay special regard to those who, by the accidents of time, or place, or circumstance, are brought into closer connection with you.
work: On Christian Doctrine, Book 1, Chapter 28
significance: We cannot help everyone, so God's providence points our love first to the family, students and neighbours he has placed near us.

author: Augustine
text: What is love's perfection? To love our enemies, and to love them to the end that they may be our brothers.
work: Ten Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Homily 1 (Burnaby translation)
significance: Christian love aims beyond tolerating opponents; it seeks their good and hopes to see them reconciled as brothers in Christ.

author: John Calvin
text: Let this be our rule for goodwill and helpfulness, that whenever we are able to assist others we should behave as stewards who must someday give an account of ourselves.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 35
significance: Our abilities, money and time are on loan from God, so helping others is a duty we will answer for, not an optional kindness.

author: John Calvin
text: We should forever keep in mind that we must not brood on the wickedness of man, but realize that he is God's image bearer.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 38
significance: Seeing God's image in difficult people, including students and colleagues, frees us to treat them with respect instead of contempt.

author: John Calvin
text: A Christian ought to be disposed and prepared to keep in mind that he has to reckon with God every moment of his life.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 28
significance: Living before God's face in every moment, not just on Sundays, brings integrity to private choices and public work alike.

author: John Calvin
text: Since God has revealed himself as a Father, we would be guilty of the basest ingratitude if we did not behave as his children.
work: Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life (1551; van Andel translation), p. 19
significance: Holy living flows from gratitude: those adopted by a loving Father want to reflect his character as his children.

author: Martin Luther
text: We do not become righteous by doing righteous deeds but, having been made righteous, we do righteous deeds.
work: Disputation against Scholastic Theology (1517), Thesis 40
significance: Good works do not earn God's favour; they grow out of the righteousness God freely gives, which removes both pride and despair.

author: Martin Luther
text: For what must be enforced with rods and blows only will not develop into a good breed, and at best they will remain godly under such treatment no longer than while the rod is upon their back.
work: Large Catechism, The Second Commandment (Bente translation)
significance: Children and students formed only by fear obey only while watched; lasting godliness is nurtured with kindness and the fear of God.

author: Martin Luther
text: Mother love is stronger than the filth and scabbiness on a child, and so the love of God toward us is stronger than the dirt that clings to us.
work: Table Talk, no. 94
significance: As a parent loves a messy child, God's love for his people is greater than their sin, which should shape how we love our own children.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, to ask myself, at the end of every day, week, month, and year, wherein I could possibly, in any respect, have done better.
work: Resolutions, No. 41
significance: Regular honest self-review, done before God, turns ordinary days into steady growth in character, work and leadership.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Resolved, that I will live so, as I shall wish I had done when I come to die.
work: Resolutions, No. 17
significance: Remembering our deathbed clarifies today's priorities, putting faith, family and faithfulness ahead of passing concerns.

author: Jonathan Edwards
text: Let there be something of benevolence in all that I speak.
work: Resolutions, No. 70
significance: Our words, at home, in class and in meetings, should always carry goodwill toward others, even when they must correct or confront.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: The practice of truth is the most profitable reading of it.
work: Morning and Evening, entry for June 20
significance: Scripture does us the most good when we obey it; knowing the Bible without living it misses its purpose.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: If you tell your troubles to God, you put them into the grave; they will never rise again when you have committed them to Him. If you roll your burden anywhere else, it will roll back again like the stone of Sisyphus.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 596
significance: Worry and complaint only bring our burdens back; prayer hands them to the one who can actually carry them.

author: Charles Spurgeon
text: The truest lengthening of life is to live while we live, wasting no time but using every hour for the highest ends. So be it this day.
work: Faith's Checkbook, entry for June 22
significance: A full life is measured by how well its hours are spent for God, not by its length, so today is the day to live purposefully.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: Tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead.
work: Orthodoxy, Chapter 4, "The Ethics of Elfland"
significance: Wise leaders and teachers listen to the faithful generations before them instead of assuming the present always knows best.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: Courage is almost a contradiction in terms. It means a strong desire to live taking the form of a readiness to die.
work: Orthodoxy, Chapter 6, "The Paradoxes of Christianity"
significance: Echoing Christ's call to lose life to save it, true courage holds life dear yet is willing to lay it down for what is right.

author: G. K. Chesterton
text: The Bible tells us to love our neighbors, and also to love our enemies; probably because they are generally the same people.
work: The Illustrated London News, 16 July 1910
significance: The hardest people to love are often the ones closest to us, so Christ's command to love enemies starts at home and work.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen. Not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.
work: "Is Theology Poetry?" (1945 address to the Oxford Socratic Club)
significance: Christianity is not just one belief among many but the light that makes sense of all of life, learning and work.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: A proud man is always looking down on things and people: and, of course, as long as you are looking down, you cannot see something that is above you.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 3, Chapter 8, "The Great Sin"
significance: Pride blinds us to God; looking down on others keeps us from looking up to the one who is above us all.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: If I find in myself a desire which no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 3, Chapter 10, "Hope"
significance: Our unsatisfied longings point beyond this life to God and heaven, freeing us from demanding that earthly things fill us completely.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: The hardness of God is kinder than the softness of men, and His compulsion is our liberation.
work: Surprised by Joy, Chapter 14, "Checkmate"
significance: When God presses hard on us, it is for our freedom and good, unlike indulgent human kindness that leaves us unchanged.

author: C. S. Lewis
text: God cannot give us a happiness and peace apart from Himself, because it is not there. There is no such thing.
work: Mere Christianity, Book 2, Chapter 3, "The Shocking Alternative"
significance: Lasting peace is found only in God himself, so seeking happiness anywhere else, even in good gifts, will always fall short.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: We must be ready to allow ourselves to be interrupted by God. God will be constantly crossing our paths and canceling our plans by sending us people with claims and petitions.
work: Life Together, Chapter 4, "Ministry"
significance: The child, student or colleague who interrupts our plans may be God's assignment for the day, not an obstacle to our real work.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: It is not your love that sustains the marriage, but from now on, the marriage that sustains your love.
work: Letters and Papers from Prison, "A Wedding Sermon from a Prison Cell" (May 1943)
significance: Marriage is a covenant God establishes, and keeping its promises carries a couple through seasons when feelings run low.

author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
text: The will of God, to which the law gives expression, is that men should defeat their enemies by loving them.
work: The Cost of Discipleship, "The Enemy, the Extraordinary", p. 147
significance: Christians overcome hostility not by retaliation but by active love, which is the costly way Christ defeated his own enemies.

author: Herman Bavinck
text: Christians may not permit their conduct to be determined by the spirit of the age, but must focus on the requirement of God's commandment
work: The Christian Family (1908; English tr. 2012)
significance: Families and schools are shaped by cultural trends, but Christians take their direction from God's word, not the mood of the moment.

author: Herman Bavinck
text: The history of the human race begins with a wedding
work: The Christian Family (1908; English tr. 2012)
significance: God himself established marriage at the start of history, giving husbands and wives a calling central to his purposes for the world.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: The world's idea of greatness is to rule, but Christian greatness consists in serving.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. Mark, on Mark 9:30-37
significance: Christ redefines leadership: the greatest in his kingdom are those who serve others, not those who hold the most power.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Our Lord has many weak children in His family, many dull pupils in His school, many raw soldiers in His army, and many lame sheep in His flock. Yet He bears with them all, and casts none away.
work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. John, Vol. 3, on John 20:24-31
significance: Christ's patience with slow, struggling disciples comforts us and models how teachers and parents should bear with those in their care.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: The Bible in the pulpit must never supersede the Bible at home.
work: Holiness, Chapter 19, "Wants of the Times"
significance: Good preaching cannot replace a father's and mother's own reading and teaching of Scripture in the home.

author: J. C. Ryle
text: Fear puts an end to openness of manner; fear leads to concealment; fear sows the seed of much hypocrisy, and leads to many a lie.
work: The Upper Room, Chapter 16, "The Duties of Parents"
significance: Children ruled by fear learn to hide and pretend, so parents and teachers should lead with love that invites honesty.

author: John Owen
text: Sin always aims at the utmost; every time it rises up to tempt or entice, if it had its own way, it would go to the very worst sin of that kind.
original: Sin aims always at the utmost; every time it rises up to tempt or entice, might it have its own course, it would go out to the utmost sin in that kind.
work: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, Chapter 2 (modernized)
significance: Small sins are never harmless, because every temptation aims at full ruin; wisdom deals with them early and seriously.

author: John Owen
text: Indeed, just as your great worry is about the Father's love, so there is no way you can trouble or burden him more than by unkindly refusing to believe in it.
original: Yea, as your great trouble is about the Father's love, so you can no way more trouble or burden him, than by your unkindness in not believing of it.
work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, Part 1, Chapter 3 (modernized)
significance: Doubting the Father's love grieves him; believers honour God by resting in his love rather than questioning it.

author: Richard Baxter
text: Many a tailor goes about in rags while making costly clothes for others; and many a cook barely licks his fingers after preparing the most costly dishes for others.
original: Many a tailor goes in rags, that maketh costly clothes for others; and many a cook scarcely licks his fingers, when he hath dressed for others the most costly dishes.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1 (modernized)
significance: Those who feed others spiritually, as pastors, teachers and parents, can starve their own souls; we must take the truth we give.

author: Richard Baxter
text: Do not be content with being in a state of grace, but take care also that your graces are kept in vigorous, lively exercise, and that you preach to yourselves the sermons you study before you preach them to others.
original: Content not yourselves with being in a state of grace, but be also careful that your graces are kept in vigorous and lively exercise, and that you preach to yourselves the sermons which you study, before you preach them to others.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1 (modernized)
significance: Anyone who teaches others must first apply the lesson to their own heart, keeping their faith active rather than merely professional.

author: Richard Baxter
text: God never saved any man for being a preacher, nor because he was an able preacher; but because he was a justified, sanctified man, and consequently faithful in his Master's work.
work: The Reformed Pastor, Chapter 1, Section 1
significance: Gifts and positions do not make us right with God; only grace does, and faithful service flows from that grace.

author: Thomas Watson
text: The two great graces essential to a saint in this life are faith and repentance. These are the two wings by which he flies to heaven.
work: The Doctrine of Repentance (1668)
significance: Trusting Christ and turning from sin belong together; the Christian life needs both, as a bird needs two wings.

author: Thomas Watson
text: Our work is great, our time short, our Master urgent.
work: The Christian Soldier; or Heaven Taken by Storm (1669)
significance: With much to do for God and limited time, believers should pursue their calling with focus and earnestness.

author: Thomas Watson
text: Nothing can hurt the soul but sin. Affliction does not hurt it; it often makes it better, as the furnace makes gold purer. It is sin that does the damage.
original: There is nothing that can hurt the soul but sin; it is not affliction that hurts it, it often makes it better, as the furnace makes gold the purer; but it is sin that damnifies.
work: A Body of Divinity (1692), "Christ the Redeemer" (modernized)
significance: Hardship can refine us like gold in a furnace; the real danger to the soul is sin, not suffering.

author: John Bunyan
text: He that is down, needs fear no fall; / He that is low, no pride: / He that is humble, ever shall / Have God to be his guide.
work: The Pilgrim's Progress, Part 2 (the shepherd boy's song)
significance: Humility brings security and contentment, because God guides those who do not trust in their own height.

author: John Bunyan
text: My sword I give to him that shall succeed me in my pilgrimage, and my courage and skill to him that can get it.
work: The Pilgrim's Progress, Part 2 (Mr. Valiant-for-truth)
significance: Faithful believers pass on their tools and example to the next generation, who must then earn courage and skill for themselves.

author: John Bunyan
text: The soul of religion is the practical part.
work: The Pilgrim's Progress, Part 1 (Christian on Talkative)
significance: Talking well about faith is empty without obedience; genuine religion shows itself in how we actually live.

author: Thomas Brooks
text: Precepts may instruct, but examples persuade.
work: Heaven on Earth (1654)
significance: Parents, teachers and leaders shape others most by how they live, so their example must reinforce their words.

author: Thomas Brooks
text: An excellent master is always better than an excellent law. Let your laws be ever so good, if the lawmakers are bad, all will come to nothing.
work: Heaven on Earth (1654)
significance: Good rules and systems cannot replace godly character in those who lead; leaders' integrity matters more than policies.

author: Thomas Brooks
text: The lives of such are most desirable, and the deaths of such will be most lamented, who make it their business to serve their generation.
work: A Cabinet of Jewels
significance: A life spent serving the people of our own day for God's sake is the kind most valued and most missed.

author: Matthew Henry
text: ... not made out of his head to rule over him, nor out of his feet to be trampled upon by him, but out of his side to be equal with him, under his arm to be protected, and near his heart to be beloved.
work: Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Genesis 2:21
significance: A husband is called to honour, protect and cherish his wife as his equal and beloved partner, never to dominate or demean her.

author: Matthew Henry
text: Whatever we have, the property of it is God's; we have only the use of it, according to the direction of our great Lord, and for his honour.
work: Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Luke 16
significance: We are managers, not owners, of everything we have, so money, time and talents should be used as God directs and for his glory.

author: Matthew Henry
text: Extraordinary afflictions are not always the punishment of extraordinary sins, but sometimes the trial of extraordinary graces.
work: As quoted in Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 9
significance: Severe suffering is not proof of God's anger; like Job's trials, it may be God strengthening and displaying deep faith.

author: Francis Schaeffer
text: His death there on Calvary's cross is for us individually, but it's not egotistically individualistic. Our individual salvation will one day be a portion of the restoration of all things.
work: "A Christian Manifesto" (1982 lecture, Coral Ridge Presbyterian Church)
significance: Personal salvation is part of God's plan to renew all creation, which gives meaning to Christian work for healing in every area of life.
